entities.summary:
Irish Sea is the largest sea in the British Isles, separating Great Britain from Ireland. It plays a crucial role in the region's maritime history, with the earliest recorded navigation dating back to the Mesolithic era. The sea's significance extends to its impact on the development of Celtic cultures and trade networks, particularly during the Classical era of empires and foundational civilizations.

The Irish Sea has been a vital trade route for centuries, with the ancient Romans using it to establish connections with the Roman province of Britannia. The sea's strategic location also made it a key battleground during the Norman conquest of Ireland in the 12th century. Furthermore, the Irish Sea has been an important hub for fishing and shipbuilding industries, with many notable vessels having set sail from its ports.

The legacy of the Irish Sea can be seen in its ongoing role as a major shipping route, with many of the world's largest container ships passing through its waters. The sea's rich cultural heritage is also reflected in its numerous historical sites, including the ancient fortresses of Rathlin Island and the medieval town of Carrickfergus.

One striking statistic that highlights the Irish Sea's enduring significance is the fact that it is home to over 200 islands, many of which are still uninhabited today. The sea's unique combination of geography and climate has created a diverse range of ecosystems, from the rocky shores of the Antrim Coast to the sandy beaches of the Donegal Peninsula.

The Irish Sea's impact on the environment is also a pressing concern, with pollution and overfishing threatening the delicate balance of its ecosystems. Efforts to protect the sea's marine life and habitats are ongoing, with conservation organizations working to establish marine protected areas and reduce plastic pollution.
